questions.title: Does Louisiana law require a signature on the premium‐finance company’ s notice of cancellation?
questions.question_body: In Williams v. GoAuto, the court held that the statute’s use of the word “certifying” does not mandate a signature. However, prior decisions like Benitez v. Elsayed mention that the notice was ‘not signed by any individual.’ How does Louisiana jurisprudence interpret the requirement for a signature (or lack thereof) under § 9:3550(G)(3)(a)?

questions.title: What does “receipt” mean in the context of a cancellation notice sent electronically?
questions.question_body: The court uses Black’s Law Dictionary definitions of receipt to conclude that an e‑mail to GoAuto’s computer system constitutes receipt. Has Louisiana law ever defined or clarified the term “receipt” for electronic communications in insurance cancellation contexts? Is the court’s reading consistent with earlier cases or modern statutory interpretation principles?

questions.title: Is a shared filing cabinet sufficient for “receipt” under the cancellation statute?
questions.question_body: The opinion notes that before 2017 the filing cabinet was owned by GoAuto Management Services, and after 2017 an APAC employee stamps the document as “received” before placing it in a shared cabinet. Do courts treat possession of a physical document in a shared space as satisfying the statute’s receipt requirement, or does actual hand‑off to a GoAuto employee need to occur?

questions.title: Why did the court not certify the statutory questions to the Louisiana Supreme Court?
questions.question_body: Williams v. GoAuto emphasizes that certification is a scarce resource and is reserved for compelling cases. The court cites Jefferson v. Lead Indus. Ass’n to justify denial. What threshold of importance or divisiveness does a Sixth Circuit case need to meet to warrant certification to the Louisiana Supreme Court?

questions.title: How does the Louisiana Supreme Court’s definition of a “private carrier” influence cancellation notice requirements?
questions.question_body: The district court identified an APAC employee as a private carrier, drawing an analogy from a Fifth Circuit case (Huntley v. Bayer). Has the Louisiana Supreme Court addressed what constitutes a private carrier in insurance‑financing contexts, and could a different interpretation materially affect whether GoAuto’s notices complied with § 9:3550(G)(3)(a)(ii)?

questions.title: Does the statutory requirement for notifying all interested parties still apply when the insurer cancels electronically?
questions.question_body: Clause (iv) of § 9:3550(G)(3)(a) requires copies of the notice to be sent to all persons listed in the finance agreement. The court accepts an e‑mail sent by APAC to GoAuto as satisfying this. Is an electronic notice sent to the insurer considered a valid method of notifying all interested parties, or must copies be sent directly to each interested person?

questions.title: What standard of proof is required for a summary judgment motion in statutory compliance disputes?
questions.question_body: The district court granted GoAuto’s summary judgment motion, concluding its cancellation procedures complied with Louisiana law. What evidentiary standard must a party meet to establish compliance or non‑compliance with an insurance‑policy cancellation statute when the dispute centers on procedural details?
